title: Keep the Best, Forget the Rest: Reliable Alignment with Order-Aware Preference Optimization
claim: Misaligned reference-policy samples are common at every model scale and hurt training, but a simple modification recovers performance.
layout: 2 panels, side-by-side grouped bar charts, three model sizes each
description: Two grouped bar charts sit side by side, each comparing three model sizes (GPT-small, GPT-med, GPT-large) on the x-axis. Panel A, titled 'Reference Model Performance', plots sample counts from 0 to about 1000 in salmon (Correct) and sky-blue (Wrong) bars. The Wrong bars are taller for small and medium models and roughly equal to Correct for large, so misaligned data persists at every size. Panel B, titled 'Reward Scores', plots reward from 1.0 to 1.7 in orange (DPO) and green (RAPPO) bars. RAPPO is slightly higher than DPO at every size, with the largest gap for GPT-large. Legends sit in the top-left corner of each panel. The eye goes first to the colored bar pairs and the rising bars in B.
caption: (A) Reference model performance across three SFT models (GPT2-Small, Medium, and Large). Correct: the reference policy aligns with human preference. Wrong: the reference policy conflicts with human preference. (A) shows that misaligned data are frequent regardless of model size, though the proportion decreases as model size increases. (B) Reward scores on the IMDb experiment (Section 5.1) using DPO and RAPPO under different reference policy scales. Performance declines as the reference policy weakens. Nonetheless, with a simple modification to DPO, our method RAPPO improves performance by 3.5%, 1.1%, and 7.1% across the three models.
abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has emerged as a powerful framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences via pairwise comparisons. However, its performance is highly sensitive to the quality of training samples: when the reference policy is poorly aligned with human preferences, ambiguous pairs can dominate the gradient signal and degrade generalization. To address this, we propose RAPPO($\textbf{R}$eliable $\textbf{A}$lignment for $\textbf{P}$reference $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{O}$ptimization), a simple sample-aware modification of the DPO loss that mitigates reference-policy misalignment by filtering out the hardest, most ambiguous samples. We theoretically show that RAPPO yields improved generalization guarantees. RAPPO is lightweight and requires only a few lines of code to be integrated into any existing DPO-type algorithm. Surprisingly, With this simple modification, our simulations across a broad suite of alignment tasks and benchmarks show consistent gains over DPO and recent state-of-the-art baselines. On the PKU-SafeRLHF benchmark, RAPPO attains helpfulness $0.693$ ($+34.8\%$ over DPO) and harmlessness $0.357$ ($-21.0\%$ vs DPO).
